In summer, {lea|ves} look {gr|een} because {th|ey} are full of chlorophyll, a substance that {he|lps} plants make {fo|od} from sunlight. When the {da|ys} get shorter, trees {slo|wly} stop making chlorophyll. As the green {co|lor} fades, yellow and orange colors that {we|re} {hid|den} in the leaf all along become easy to see. Some trees also make new red colors from sugar that stays inside their leaves.

4.5.paragraph: Every autumn, the leaves of many trees change from green to bright yellow, orange, and red. {Dur|ing} the growing {sea|son}, leaves {con|tain} large amounts of chlorophyll, the green {pig|ment} that captures sunlight {f|or} photosynthesis. As days {bec|ome} shorter and nights grow {coo|ler}, trees {grad|ually} stop producing chlorophyll and break {do|wn} what {rem|ains}. This allows yellow and orange pigments, which were present all summer, to become visible. In some species, sugars trapped in the leaves are used to produce red pigments.

5.5.paragraph: The brilliant colors of autumn foliage result largely from chemical changes that begin as a tree prepares for winter. {Throu|ghout} the summer, chlorophyll {domi|nates} the leaf, {mas|king} other pigments such as {carot|enoids}, which reflect yellow and orange light. As daylight {dimin|ishes}, deciduous trees {ce|ase} synthesizing chlorophyll and {reab|sorb} its valuable {nutr|ients}. {Conseq|uently}, these yellow pigments are {reve|aled}. Certain species, including many maples, additionally produce anthocyanins, red pigments thought to shield leaves from excess light while nutrients are recovered.

shared.title: The Early Days of Photography
shared.text:
Although the camera obscura, a dark box or room that projects an image through a small hole, had been known for centuries, no one could make its images permanent until the 1820s. Around 1826, the French inventor Joseph Nicéphore Niépce coated a metal plate with a light-sensitive substance and placed it in a camera aimed out of his window. The result, now considered the oldest surviving camera photograph, required an exposure of many hours, so the buildings in it appear to be lit by the sun from both sides.

In 1839, Niépce's former partner, Louis Daguerre, introduced a far more practical process. His daguerreotypes, made on polished silver-coated copper plates, captured remarkably fine detail and needed exposures of only minutes. However, each daguerreotype was a unique object; it could not be copied.

Around the same time, the English scientist William Henry Fox Talbot developed a different approach. His process produced a paper negative from which any number of positive prints could be made. Talbot's images were less sharp than daguerreotypes, because the fibers of the paper blurred fine details. Nevertheless, the principle of making many prints from a single negative proved enormously influential, and it shaped photography for more than a century and a half.

shared.title: Talking with an advisor about changing majors

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: Hi, Ms. Rivera. I have a two o'clock appointment. I'm thinking about changing my major.

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: Sure, have a seat. You're in mechanical engineering right now, right? What are you thinking of switching to?

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: Environmental science. I took the intro course this semester as an elective, and honestly, it's the only class I look forward to.

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: That's a good sign. Have you looked at the requirements for the environmental science program?

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: A little. I know I'd need biology and chemistry. I've already taken general chemistry, though.

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: Good, that counts for both programs. And your calculus and physics courses would count as electives, so you wouldn't lose much credit.

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: Really? I was worried I'd have to add an extra year.

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: Probably just one extra semester, maybe less if you take a summer course. The tricky part is biology. The first course is only offered in the fall, and it fills up fast.

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: So I should sign up the day registration opens?

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: Exactly. And before you officially switch, I'd suggest talking with a professor in the department. They can tell you what kinds of jobs graduates usually get.

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: That makes sense. I'll email the department this week and set up a meeting.

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: Great. Once you've decided, bring me the change-of-major form and I'll sign it.

shared.title: Guest lecture series
shared.speaker: Student activities coordinator
shared.text: Good morning, everyone. I have a quick announcement about this semester's guest lecture series. Starting next week, we'll host a speaker every Wednesday evening at seven in the main auditorium. This year's theme is science in everyday life, and the first talk is about the chemistry of cooking. The lectures are free and open to everyone, but seating is limited, so please reserve a seat through the student portal. If you can't make it, don't worry. Each lecture will be recorded and posted online within a week. Also, students who attend at least three lectures and turn in a short written reflection will receive a certificate of participation, which you can list on your resume. Oh, and one more thing: after each talk, there'll be a reception where you can meet the speaker and ask questions. Hope to see you there!

shared.question: Many cities are trying to reduce traffic and air pollution in their downtown areas. Some planners have proposed banning private cars from city centers entirely, allowing only public transit, bicycles, delivery vehicles, and emergency services. Should city centers ban private cars? Why or why not?

posts.name: Priya
posts.text: I support a ban. Without cars, streets could be turned into wider sidewalks, bike lanes, and outdoor seating, which would make downtown areas safer and more pleasant for pedestrians. Cleaner air is another major benefit. People would adjust quickly, especially if cities used the money saved on road maintenance to improve buses and trains.

posts.name: Daniel
posts.text: A complete ban seems unfair to me. Older people, parents with young children, and people with disabilities often depend on cars to get around. Also, many small businesses downtown rely on customers who drive in from the suburbs. I think a better solution would be higher parking fees or limits on cars during the busiest hours.
